title: International Economics Adventure 3: Trade Blocs & WTO
welcome_lead: Today you'll trace the ladder from a free trade area to monetary union and meet the WTO.
meta_desc: Economics: ladder of integration (FTA, customs union, common market, monetary union) and WTO.
final_note: You ranked integration types and outlined the WTO's role in trade rules.

concepts.def: Free trade area — no internal tariffs
Switch from costly home to cheap partner
Switch from cheap non-member to costly member

walkthroughs.body_html:
Five rungs of trade integration.

1. FTA — no internal tariffs (e.g. USMCA).
2. Customs union — common external tariff (Mercosur).
3. Common market — free movement of goods, labour, capital (EU Single Market).
4. Monetary union — shared currency (Eurozone).
5. Political/economic union — common policy.

Trade creation: tariffs fall, members switch from costly home producers to cheaper partners — welfare ↑.

Trade diversion: a previously cheaper non-member is now blocked by the common tariff — welfare ↓.

Net welfare depends on which effect dominates.

The World Trade Organization (1995, succeeding GATT 1947) sets multilateral rules.

Core principles: most-favoured nation, national treatment, tariff binding, dispute settlement.

Doha round (2001) on development largely stalled; the Appellate Body is currently paralysed.

mcqs.q: What determines the size of the fiscal multiplier?
options: Demand always falls when supply increases.
Mainly the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) — the higher the share of extra income people spend domestically, the bigger the multiplier. Leakages (saving, imports, taxes) reduce the multiplier.
The fiscal multiplier is always 2 or 3.
The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a shift in demand and a movement along the demand curve?
options: A change in price shifts the demand curve.
A movement along the curve is caused by a change in price; a shift of the whole curve is caused by changes in other factors (income, tastes, substitute prices).
The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.
Demand always falls when supply increases.

mcqs.q: What is the principle of comparative advantage?
options: Comparative advantage means richer countries should help poorer ones.
Countries should specialise in producing goods with lower opportunity cost relative to others — even a country worse at everything still has a comparative advantage in something.
Demand always falls when supply increases.
A country should produce whatever it can make best.
